messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Public Transport: Bus riding, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Kiet was 27 when he first came to treatment, a South Eastern Asian American journalist living with his boyfriend in a small apartment near the train line. He described the period of abuse by a previous romantic partner as something that had unfolded behind ordinary routines, beginning with criticism and control and eventually turning physical. The most vivid memories were not of a single dramatic moment but of being grabbed, shoved, and hurt in ways that left him feeling trapped and embarrassed to name what was happening. Even now, when he spoke about those months, his account would tighten around specific details: the sound of a door closing too hard, being cornered in a room, the sense that he had to keep himself small and quiet to avoid making things worse. At the time, he had not told many people, and he had tried to convince himself that he could manage it on his own.

After the relationship ended, Kiet began to notice that certain situations pulled him back into that time with a force that startled him. Being alone with men was especially difficult. If he found himself in an elevator, a stairwell, or an empty office corridor with another man, he became acutely aware of body position, exits, and the tone of voice being used around him. He described a persistent sense that harm could come from someone he had no reason to suspect. Public transport became another source of distress, especially bus rides. A crowded bus could leave him feeling cornered, but even a quieter ride could become unbearable if a man sat too close or if someone stood behind him for too long. As a journalist, he often had to travel around the city for interviews and field work, and he found himself planning routes around bus stops, sometimes taking longer commutes just to avoid a ride that might leave him feeling unsafe. On workdays, this could mean arriving tense and late, already exhausted by the effort of getting there.

He also noticed that waiting for something to happen, especially when something took longer than expected, quickly became intolerable. If a source did not reply when expected, if a ride was late, or if his boyfriend was delayed coming home, Kiet found himself assuming that something bad was happening. In those moments he would check his phone repeatedly, pace the apartment, and feel unable to settle until he had proof that everything was all right. At night, he often woke to check whether he was safe. Sometimes this meant sitting up in the dark and listening for sounds in the hallway; other times he simply looked around the room and took stock of where he was before trying to go back to sleep. Even when friends or his boyfriend reassured him that he was safe, he said it was impossible to fully believe them. Their words reached him intellectually, but not in a way that changed how his body reacted.

When memories came back, they did not feel distant or completed. Kiet described them as happening now, as if he were back in the room where he had been hurt. He would be struck by a wave of emotion so intense that he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes setting down his pen or leaving an interview notes app open on his phone while he waited for the feeling to pass. He said the memories could also bring physical pain in the same parts of his body that had been hurt before, which made the experience feel even more immediate and difficult to dismiss. He had learned to cut himself off quickly when this happened, not wanting to be overwhelmed in front of other people or lose control at work.

Over time, Kiet’s ways of coping became increasingly restrictive. He dwelled on what he had done wrong, replaying arguments and moments from the past with a harsh, self-critical focus. He often asked himself whether he had missed warning signs or somehow allowed the abuse to continue, and this rumination could last for hours. He also never allowed himself to feel or express anger. He had grown up valuing restraint, and after the abuse he made that restraint absolute, believing that anger was dangerous and unhelpful, something that had to be buried before it could show. Eating became another area of control. He would avoid eating or restrict food when he felt unsettled, describing it as a way to cope by making himself feel less occupied by his body. Friends noticed that he sometimes skipped meals during long reporting days, and his boyfriend began to comment on how little he ate, though Kiet tended to brush this off.

Beneath all of this, Kiet had come to believe that people could not be trusted and that you could never know who would harm you. He applied that belief broadly, not only to strangers but to situations that should have felt ordinary, including work interviews and social settings. He also saw himself as inadequate, someone who had somehow failed to protect himself and who now had to live with the consequences. What finally brought him to seek help was the strain of feeling constantly on guard while trying to maintain his job and his relationship. He was tired of waking in the night, tired of planning his life around buses and men he might have to stand near, and tired of feeling that reassurance never quite reached him. What he hoped for was not to erase the past, but to be able to move through a day without feeling that danger was always just about to begin.
